question: Many coins have tiny ridges around their edge. They are not there for grip. What were they originally meant to stop people from doing?
source_excerpt: Some gold and silver coins were reeded to discourage clipping, i.e. scraping off the precious metals from the edge of the coin, to maintain its stated value in precious metal.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has run a thumbnail along a coin's ridged edge, and most assume it is for grip or decoration. The real reason is a centuries-old anti-fraud measure against people shaving precious metal off coins. It still survives on coins that contain no precious metal at all.
extra.verification_notes: Reeded edges were introduced to deter clipping/shaving of precious metal from coin edges, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reeding

explanation: When coins were real gold and silver, crooks would trim slivers off the edges and melt them down, and a ridged rim made any clipping instantly visible. Isaac Newton himself championed the idea while running England's Royal Mint.

question: The word 'dollar' comes from a silver coin called the 'thaler', named after the valley where its silver was mined. In which present-day country is that valley?
source_excerpt: German Taler, shortened from Joachimstaler, a coin made in Sankt Joachimsthal

extra.why_interesting: The dollar feels like the most American thing imaginable, so players assume its name is American or at least English. In fact it traces back to a silver-mining valley in Central Europe. Most people who know about the 'thaler' will guess Germany, and the actual answer is the Czech Republic.
extra.verification_notes: Thaler derives from Joachimstaler, minted at Joachimsthal (now Jáchymov), Czech Republic, per Merriam-Webster.

explanation: The coin was the Joachimsthaler, minted from silver dug at Joachimsthal in Bohemia, today the spa town of Jáchymov in Czechia. 'Thal' simply means 'valley', so the US dollar is, quite literally, a 'valley-er'.
